title: Where Are Kazakhstan's Schools, Teachers and Students?
desc: Rural areas account for a larger share of Kazakhstan's teachers than students. Aggregate teacher numbers alone are therefore insufficient to assess staffing adequacy, the distribution of specialist expertise, or institutional support.
note: In December 2024, rural schools represented 67% of Kazakhstan's schools. The figures displayed here refer to 2026. The difference between the two reported percentages should not be interpreted as evidence of school closures. Urban percentages are calculated as complements of the reported rural shares.
source: Ministry of Education figures reported by Qazinform (2026).

title: Fewer Students per Teacher Does Not Necessarily Mean Better Institutional Support
sub: Average number of students per teacher in public day schools, Kazakhstan, 2023.
desc: Rural schools have fewer students per teacher on average than urban schools. This reinforces the need to investigate the distribution of specialist expertise and professional support rather than treating institutional inequality solely as an overall shortage of teachers.
note: Student-to-teacher ratios are not equivalent to class sizes and do not capture shortages of teachers in particular subjects or schools.
source: Kazakhstan National Report on the State and Development of the Education System (2024), pp. 145–146, Kazakh edition. Data for 2023.

title: Same Profession, Different Qualification Profiles
sub: Professional qualification categories among public-school teachers, 2023.
desc: Urban public-school teachers are more frequently represented in the two highest professional qualification categories. Rural teachers have higher shares in the teacher, moderator and expert categories.
note: Three legacy qualification categories from the previous qualification system are excluded. Professional qualifications measure formal professional advancement rather than actual teaching effectiveness.
source: National Education Database (2023), Kazakhstan National Education Report, Figure 2.2.30.

title: Does School Location Influence Access to Training?
sub: Mean percentage of teachers receiving training in online teaching and learning, as reported by school leaders, 2021.
desc: During the COVID-19 pandemic, urban school leaders reported significantly higher teacher participation in digital pedagogy training than rural school leaders.
note: These are average school-level participation estimates reported by school leaders rather than percentages calculated from individual teacher records. The data reflect pandemic-era conditions and do not necessarily represent current geographical disparities.

title: Having a Mentoring Programme Does Not Mean Having a Mentor
sub: Mentoring arrangements among novice lower-secondary teachers, 2024.
desc: Kazakhstan exceeds the OECD average in mentoring provision. Nevertheless, only 43% of novice teachers have an assigned mentor, illustrating a distinction between institutional programme availability and individualized support.
note: The 2018 value is reconstructed from the published 2024 percentage and reported change. These are national indicators and do not distinguish rural from urban schools.

title: What Prevents Teachers from Accessing Professional Development?
sub: Percentage of teachers reporting selected barriers, Kazakhstan, 2024.
desc: Teachers identify financial and time-related constraints as important barriers to professional learning. These findings provide a rationale for investigating more affordable and flexible forms of professional support.
note: These are self-reported national-level indicators. Responses are not mutually exclusive. The data do not establish that AI would necessarily overcome these barriers.

title: What Professional Support Do Teachers Need?
sub: Percentage of teachers reporting a high level of professional learning need, Kazakhstan, 2024.
desc: Curriculum knowledge and digital teaching skills are among the most frequently reported areas of high professional learning need in Kazakhstan.
note: These percentages represent self-reported professional learning needs rather than objectively measured skill deficiencies.

title: Kazakhstan's Teachers Are Already Using AI
sub: Percentage of lower-secondary teachers reporting AI use in their work, 2024.
desc: Reported AI use among lower-secondary teachers in Kazakhstan exceeds the OECD average, indicating that AI is already integrated into some professional activities.
note: AI adoption should not be confused with AI literacy, technological readiness or effective AI use.

title: Beyond Automation: AI as a Professional Resource
sub: Reported activities among teachers using AI in Kazakhstan, 2024.
desc: AI is already used for activities relevant to instructional preparation and professional learning. However, the frequency of reported use does not demonstrate its educational effectiveness.
note: Percentages refer to teachers who reported using AI. Activities are not mutually exclusive.

title: Could AI Reinforce Existing Inequalities?
sub: Reported barriers among teachers who had not used AI in teaching, 2024.
desc: Among teachers who had not used AI in teaching, inadequate school infrastructure was more frequently reported as a barrier in Kazakhstan than the OECD average. This highlights the importance of addressing technological accessibility when designing AI-assisted teacher support.
note: These percentages refer specifically to teachers who had not used AI in their teaching during the preceding 12 months. They do not establish whether infrastructure problems are more prevalent in rural schools.
